alt: Speed-time graph of a car pulling away: speed rises in a straight line from 0 to 18 m/s in 7.5 s, so the gradient, which is the acceleration, is 2.4 m/s squared (every 3 s the speed rises by 7.2 m/s); after 7.5 s the speed stays at 18 m/s.
caption: Figure: the gradient of a speed-time graph is the acceleration

alt: Two sketches of a tall block tilted about its bottom corner. At 15 degrees the vertical line down from the centre of gravity still lands inside the base, so the weight turns the block back upright. At 45 degrees the line falls outside the base, so the weight turns the block over.
caption: Figure: an object topples when the line of its weight falls outside its base

alt: Sheet of standard circuit symbols, each labelled: cell, battery, d.c. supply, open and closed switch, lamp, fixed and variable resistor, heater, NTC thermistor, LDR, fuse, ammeter (A), voltmeter (V), motor (M), generator (G), potential divider, diode and LED.
caption: Figure: the standard circuit symbols

alt: Circuit loop with a cell and lamp: conventional current is drawn leaving the positive terminal and flowing round to the negative terminal, while the electrons in the wire drift the opposite way, from negative to positive.
caption: Figure: conventional current and electron flow go opposite ways

alt: End view of a d.c. motor coil with its plane along the magnetic field between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right. Current goes into the page on the left side and out on the right side, so Fleming's left-hand rule gives a downward force on the left and an upward force on the right, turning the coil anticlockwise.
caption: Figure: the forces on opposite sides of the coil give a turning effect

alt: Energy of a 1.0 kg stone falling 5.0 m, ignoring air resistance: at the top it has 49.0 J of potential energy and no kinetic energy; halfway down each is 24.5 J; at the bottom all 49.0 J is kinetic, a speed of 9.9 m/s. The total stays 49.0 J.
caption: Figure: potential energy changes into kinetic energy as a 1.0 kg stone falls

alt: Output of an a.c. generator against time for a coil turning 25 times a second: the e.m.f. is zero when the coil is vertical, peaks after a quarter turn (0.01 s) when the coil is horizontal, is zero again at half a turn, reaches a trough at three-quarters of a turn, and repeats every 0.04 s, a frequency of 25 Hz.
caption: Figure: one turn of the coil gives one cycle of alternating e.m.f.

alt: Decay curve for a source with a half-life of 6.0 hours and an initial count rate of 1200 counts per minute: the count rate falls to 600 after 6 hours, 300 after 12, 150 after 18 and 75 after 24 hours, halving in every equal 6-hour step, falling steeply at first and then more slowly.
caption: Figure: the count rate halves every half-life

alt: Heating curve for water heated steadily: temperature rises as a solid, then stays flat at 0 degrees Celsius while the ice melts, rises as a liquid, stays flat at 100 degrees Celsius while it boils, then rises again as a gas. The energy supplied during the flat sections breaks bonds instead of raising the temperature.
caption: Figure: the temperature stays constant while a substance melts or boils

alt: Load-extension graph for a spring: a straight line through the origin up to 6 N (a spring with 4.0 N giving 4.0 cm, so k = 100 N per m), then the line curves upwards beyond the limit of proportionality, where Hooke's law no longer applies.
caption: Figure: extension is proportional to load up to the limit of proportionality

alt: Two current-voltage graphs. Filament lamp: an S-shaped curve through the origin that gets less steep as V increases, in both directions, because the hot filament has higher resistance. Diode: almost no current for negative V and below about 0.6 V, then the current rises steeply.
caption: Figure: I-V graphs of a filament lamp and a diode

alt: Current-voltage graph of a fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin, reaching 0.40 A at 12 V; the current is proportional to the p.d., so the resistance is constant at 30 ohms (12 V divided by 0.40 A).
caption: Figure: an ohmic conductor gives a straight I-V line

alt: Circuit diagram: a cell, closed switch, ammeter and lamp in a single series loop, with a voltmeter connected in parallel across the lamp; the ammeter measures the current through the lamp and the voltmeter the p.d. across it.
caption: Figure: an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel with the lamp

alt: Ray diagram for a converging lens with the object beyond 2F (200 units from the lens, focal length 80): a ray parallel to the axis passes through the far focus and a ray through the centre goes straight on; they meet at a real image 133 units behind the lens, inverted and diminished.
caption: Figure: converging lens with the object beyond 2F

alt: Ray diagram for a converging lens used as a magnifying glass: the object is 50 units from the lens, inside the focal length of 80. The rays leave the lens diverging; traced backwards as dashed lines they appear to come from an upright, enlarged, virtual image on the same side as the object.
caption: Figure: a converging lens as a magnifying glass

alt: Magnetic field of a bar magnet: field lines loop out of the north pole and curve round into the south pole, never crossing, and are closest together near the poles where the field is strongest.
caption: Figure: the magnetic field of a bar magnet

alt: Magnetic field of a solenoid: outside the coil the field lines loop from one end to the other like a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other; inside the coil the lines are straight, parallel and close together, so the field is strong and almost uniform.
caption: Figure: the field of a solenoid is like that of a bar magnet

alt: Magnetic field around a straight wire carrying a current towards the viewer: concentric circular field lines centred on the wire, directed anticlockwise by the right-hand grip rule, with the circles drawn further apart at greater distance because the field gets weaker.
caption: Figure: field lines around a straight current-carrying wire

alt: Uniform beam pivoted at its centre: 4.0 N hangs 30 cm to the left; 2.0 N hangs 20 cm and an unknown weight W hangs 40 cm to the right. Anticlockwise moment is 120 N cm, so 40 plus 40W equals 120 and W is 2.0 N.
caption: Figure: balancing a beam with more than one weight on a side

alt: See-saw balanced about a pivot: the child's 300 N weight acts 2.0 m to the left and her father's 750 N weight acts 0.80 m to the right. The anticlockwise moment, 300 times 2.0, is 600 N m and equals the clockwise moment, 750 times 0.80, also 600 N m.
caption: Figure: a see-saw balances when clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal

alt: Distance-time graph: a straight line from the origin to 300 m at 40 s. A gradient triangle with 150 m up and 20 s across gives the speed, 7.5 m/s, which is constant because the line is straight.
caption: Figure: the gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed

alt: Speed-time graph of a trolley: speeds up from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 s (gradient 2.0 m/s squared), moves at a steady 12 m/s for 10 s, then slows to rest in 4 s (gradient minus 3.0 m/s squared). The areas under the three sections are 36 m, 120 m and 24 m, a total distance of 180 m.
caption: Figure: gradient gives acceleration; area under the line gives distance

alt: Curved distance-time graph that gets steeper with time. A straight tangent drawn at 20 s rises 64 m over 16 s, so the speed at that instant is 4.0 m/s; the curve means the speed is increasing.
caption: Figure: a tangent to the curve gives the speed at one instant

alt: Motor effect: a wire carrying current into the page lies between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right, so the field points right. By Fleming's left-hand rule (first finger field, second finger current) the thumb points down: the wire is pushed downwards.
caption: Figure: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on the wire

alt: Optical fibre: a ray zigzags along a glass core, meeting the wall each time at an angle of incidence of 60 degrees, which is greater than the critical angle of about 42 degrees, so it is totally internally reflected every time and stays inside.
caption: Figure: light is trapped in a fibre by repeated total internal reflection

alt: Parallel circuit: a 12 V supply connected directly across a 6.0 ohm and a 3.0 ohm resistor. Each branch has 12 V across it; the branch currents are 2.0 A and 4.0 A, which add to the 6.0 A supply current. Combined resistance 2.0 ohms.
caption: Figure: same p.d. in each branch; branch currents add

alt: Plane mirror image: an object stands 1.5 m in front of a mirror and its image appears 1.5 m behind it, upright and the same size. A ray from the object reflects into the eye; extended backwards as a dashed line it meets at the virtual image.
caption: Figure: the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front

alt: Potential divider: a 2.0 kilohm and a 1.0 kilohm resistor in series across a 9.0 V supply. The p.d.s are in the ratio of the resistances, 6.0 V across the larger resistor and 3.0 V across the smaller, adding to 9.0 V.
caption: Figure: a potential divider shares 9.0 V in the ratio 2 : 1

alt: Light-sensing potential divider: a fixed resistor in series with an LDR across a 6 V supply, with a voltmeter taking the output across the LDR. In the dark the LDR's resistance is high so its share of the p.d. is high; in bright light it falls.
caption: Figure: an LDR potential divider gives a high output in the dark

alt: A 600 N crate resting on two faces: on its largest face, 0.20 square metres, it exerts a pressure of 3000 Pa; stood on its smallest face, 0.050 square metres, the same weight gives 12 000 Pa, four times the pressure from a quarter of the area.
caption: Figure: the same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure

alt: Tank of water 8.0 m deep with arrows pushing sideways on the wall that get longer with depth: pressure increases with depth. At 8.0 m, with a density of 1000 kg per cubic metre and g of 9.8 N per kg, the pressure from the water is 78 400 Pa.
caption: Figure: liquid pressure increases with depth

alt: Four voltage-time graphs over two cycles of 50 Hz mains. The a.c. input swings above and below zero. Half-wave rectification keeps only the positive humps, with gaps between them. Full-wave rectification gives a continuous row of humps, twice as many. Adding a smoothing capacitor gives an almost steady output with a small ripple.
caption: Figure: a.c. input, half-wave, full-wave and smoothed outputs

alt: Law of reflection: a ray meets a plane mirror at 35 degrees to the surface, so its angle of incidence from the normal is 55 degrees; the reflected ray leaves at 55 degrees on the other side of the normal. Angles are measured from the dashed normal, not from the mirror.
caption: Figure: angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal

alt: Ray through a glass block: entering from air at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees it bends towards the normal to an angle of refraction of 25 degrees, so the refractive index is sin 40 over sin 25, 1.52. It leaves the opposite face at 40 degrees, parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
caption: Figure: light bends towards the normal on entering glass and away on leaving

alt: Free-body diagram of a 900 kg boat: an engine thrust of 2400 N forwards and water resistance of 600 N backwards. The resultant force is 1800 N forwards, so the acceleration is 1800 divided by 900, which is 2.0 m/s squared.
caption: Figure: use the resultant force in F = ma

alt: Series circuit: a 6.0 V battery with 4.0 ohm and 8.0 ohm resistors in one loop. The same 0.50 A flows everywhere, and the p.d.s of 2.0 V and 4.0 V add up to 6.0 V.
caption: Figure: current is the same in series; p.d.s add

alt: Circuit: a 6.0 V battery in series with a lamp and a resistor; a voltmeter across each reads 4.0 V and 2.0 V, so the p.d.s across the components add up to the 6.0 V e.m.f.
caption: Figure: in series the p.d.s add up to the e.m.f.

alt: Apparatus for measuring the specific heat capacity of a 1.0 kg aluminium block: an electric heater and a thermometer in holes in the block, insulation round it, and a circuit with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the heater to find its power. A 50 W heater for 300 s supplies 15 000 J, giving a 16.5 degree rise and c of about 909 J per kg per degree Celsius.
caption: Figure: measuring the specific heat capacity of a metal block

alt: Three rays inside glass (refractive index 1.50, critical angle 41.8 degrees) meeting the glass-air boundary. At 30 degrees most light refracts out, bending away from the normal to 49 degrees; at 41.8 degrees the refracted ray skims along the surface; at 60 degrees all the light is reflected back into the glass.
caption: Figure: the critical angle separates refraction from total internal reflection

alt: Step-down transformer: a primary coil of 2000 turns connected to a 240 V a.c. supply and a secondary coil of 100 turns giving 12 V, both wound on a soft-iron core. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, 240 to 12 equals 2000 to 100.
caption: Figure: a step-down transformer with 2000 and 100 turns

alt: Velocity triangle for a boat crossing a river: 3.0 m/s straight across and 1.6 m/s downstream, drawn nose to tail. The resultant is 3.4 m/s (square root of 3.0 squared plus 1.6 squared) at 28 degrees downstream of straight across, since tan of the angle is 1.6 over 3.0.
caption: Figure: adding two velocities at right angles, nose to tail

alt: Two ripple-tank sketches of plane waves meeting a barrier with a gap. When the gap is about one wavelength wide the waves spread out into almost semicircular wavefronts; when the gap is much wider than the wavelength the waves go through nearly straight, with slight bending only at the edges. The wavelength is unchanged.
caption: Figure: diffraction is greatest when the gap is about one wavelength

alt: Longitudinal wave on a spring: the coils are drawn as vertical lines that bunch up at compressions (C) and spread apart at rarefactions (R). The vibration is along the direction the wave travels, and the wavelength is the distance between two neighbouring compressions.
caption: Figure: a longitudinal wave has compressions and rarefactions

alt: Water waves crossing from deep to shallow water at an angle: the wavefronts are closer together in the shallow region (wavelength 4.0 cm against 6.0 cm) and the ray bends towards the normal, because the waves slow from 0.30 to 0.20 m/s while the frequency stays 5.0 Hz.
caption: Figure: waves slow down in shallow water, so the wavelength shortens and they bend

alt: Transverse wave drawn as displacement against distance: crests and troughs repeat every 0.40 m, so the wavelength is 0.40 m; the amplitude is the height of a crest above the rest line. With a frequency of 2.5 Hz the wave speed is 2.5 times 0.40, 1.0 m/s.
caption: Figure: wavelength is crest to crest; amplitude is rest position to crest
